newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel, SPD see possible deal on top tax rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel, SPD see possible deal on top tax rate.

text.p: German coalition and opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leaders said on Friday there was room to compromise on the most controversial issue of planned sweeping tax reforms -- top-rate income tax.
But the two sides clashed in parliament over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to scrap a capital trading tax on companies which he said was destroying jobs.

Waigel, speaking before a second round of talks on his plan to cut 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in tax, said early agreement to cut corporation tax and the bottom rate of income tax could be a "crystallisation point" for a broader deal.

SPD opposition to a cut in the top rate to 39 percent from 53 would not survive constitutional court scrutiny, he told parliament that. If corporate taxes were cut to 35 percent from 47, the top income tax rate must fall "almost automatically".
Negotiators from both sides resumed talks which began on Monday in the search for a quick reform compromise to tackle unemployment which climbed in January to 4.7 million, the highest since 1933.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition wants a deal by Easter. Failure would condemn the measures to long wrangling in parliament, where the SPD can block tax changes through its majority in the upper house.

An early deal would allow some cuts to be brought forward to 1998, boosting the economy just as Germany struggles to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU). It would also prevent the changes falling prey to the 1998 general election campaign.

A leading SPD fiscal policy expert who joined Friday's second round of talks, North Rhine-Westphalia finance minister Heinz Schleusser, said a deal could be reached on cutting top-rate income tax but only on certain conditions.

"For me the question has always been the extent to which (such a cut) would be financed through the elimination of tax breaks," Schleusser said in a radio interview. "We have to see how far the other side is willing to go beyond that which has already been discussed, to do more."
But SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said that the top-rate tax was completely secondary to stimulating the economy and relieving the burden on productive workers.
Entering the talks, Scharping said the SPD would not yield to government plans to abolish tax relief on pay for unsocial work hours.

Schleusser, Scharping and Hamburg mayor Henning Voscherau met Waigel, Christian Democrat (CDU) parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble and his opposite number Hermann Otto Solms of the Free Democrats (FDP) in the finance ministry.

The meeting was held up slightly from its scheduled 1000 GMT start by a parliamentary debate on a government bill to scrap the capital trading tax next year. The Bundestag lower house passed the bill with a 330 to 293 majority, but the SPD said it would block the measure in the upper house.

Waigel said the tax's abolition was long overdue. "We could have abolished the capital trading tax long ago if you in the SPD had not prevented it, and then thousands of people could have been working today," he told the Bundestag.

But the SPD said the government was playing fast and loose by planning to compensate local governments for lost revenue with a share of a turnover tax without making necessary changes to the constitution.
"You want the Bundestag to pass a law which is clearly unconstitutional," SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss said. "Even if is constitutional, it violates legislative hygiene."

The capital trading tax is levied only in western Germany, and would have to be introduced automatically in the former communist east if it is not abolished. That, Waigel said, would damage the capital base of struggling companies there.
